title: UK Air Traffic Glitch Diverts Bengaluru-London Air India Flight to Vienna
excerpt: A technical fault at Britain's air traffic control provider forced Air India to divert, delay or cancel multiple UK services, as more than 1,000 flights were cancelled across Britain.
body:
• A technical fault in NATS's flight data processing system on Tuesday triggered mass disruption across UK airports, with more than 1,000 flights cancelled and further disruption spilling into Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data.
  • Air India said it had been forced to divert, delay or cancel multiple flights to and from UK airports; the Deccan Herald reported that a Bengaluru–London service was diverted to Vienna.
  • NATS said the fault was fixed by Tuesday evening, but warned that clearing the backlog would take time; Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, Stansted and Edinburgh were among the airports affected.
  • Air India warned that aircraft and crew left out of position could knock other services off schedule, and advised passengers to check their flight status before heading to the airport.

A technical fault in Britain's air traffic control system threw UK airports into chaos on Tuesday, forcing Air India to divert, delay or cancel multiple services — including a Bengaluru–London flight that was rerouted to Vienna, according to the Deccan Herald.

What Went Wrong

The UK's air traffic control provider, NATS, said a technical problem with its flight processing system disrupted departures and arrivals at major airports. More than 1,000 flights were cancelled across Britain, according to flight-tracking data, with some counts putting Tuesday's single-day cancellations above 600. By Tuesday evening NATS said normal operations had resumed: "Our system issue is now resolved. We are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights." Heathrow said it was working closely with NATS to minimise the impact on passengers and flight schedules.

Air India's Disrupted Network

In a travel advisory posted on X on September 8, Air India said: "Flights operating to and from airports in the United Kingdom have been impacted by a technical fault at NATS, the UK air traffic control provider. As a result, Air India has been forced to divert, delay or cancel multiple flights scheduled to operate to and from UK airports."

The airline apologised for the inconvenience, noting the situation was beyond its control, and warned of knock-on effects: with aircraft and crew left out of position, the disruption could extend to other services beyond the UK network.

Passengers Stranded

The scenes at British airports were chaotic: massive queues, cancelled departure boards and passengers sleeping on terminal floors. CNN reported that one family flying home to Connecticut after a holiday in Santorini was stranded at Heathrow and ended up sleeping on the airport floor with nearby hotels booked out. The disruption also hit UK–Ireland routes, with Dublin Airport warning passengers of the impact.

"Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz. It's just an absolute nightmare down there."

— Josie Donoghue, passenger stuck at Gatwick airport, to the Associated Press

What Travellers Should Do

Air India's advice stands: check your flight status before heading to the airport. Passengers on cancelled or significantly delayed services should contact the airline for rebooking, keep receipts for meals and accommodation, and check their travel insurance coverage. With crew and aircraft displaced across the network, schedules may stay fluid for several days even though NATS says its systems are back to normal.

The India–UK Corridor

The India–UK route is one of the busiest long-haul corridors for Indian travellers — students, business flyers and families visiting relatives. London is among Air India's most important international stations, so a disruption of this scale ripples straight into diaspora travel plans on both ends. With the backlog still clearing, travellers on India–UK routes this week should build in buffer time and keep monitoring airline advisories.
